# Background {#sec-background .unnumbered}

[Brains and evolution in brief]{.lb-subtitle}

This book assumes no biology and little machine learning. This page explains the few ideas that every later page
uses: what a neuron does, why some neurons excite and others inhibit, how to read the brain diagrams, the three
ways a connection gets its strength, and how evolution and the experiments are run. The parts of real brains
that the stages model are introduced on their own pages. A glossary at the end
collects the terms.

If you already know neural networks, the callout below says what is different here.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="If you know artificial neural networks"}
- The units are rate neurons: each has one activity between 0 and 1, updated once per tick, and the network is
  recurrent (a cell can feed back onto itself through others).
- Every cell is either excitatory or inhibitory: all its outgoing weights are positive, or all are negative.
- There is no backpropagation and no gradient. Weights come from three places: some are designed, most are found by
  a genetic algorithm over generations, and a few change within a life by a local learning rule.
- The networks are small (tens to a few hundred cells), and most cells have a fixed, named meaning, so that you can
  point at one and say what it is for.
- The question is not "what is the best network for this task" but "which circuit does evolution put to use,
  given the brain it already has".
:::

## Neurons and synapses

A **neuron** is a cell that collects signals from other neurons and passes on a signal of its own. In this book a
neuron is described by one number, its **activity**: 0 when it is silent, 1 when it fires as fast as it can.

Neurons are connected by **synapses**. A synapse has a **strength** (in machine learning: a weight). Every tick, a
neuron adds up the activity of the neurons that reach it, each multiplied by the strength of its synapse, and its
new activity follows that sum, squashed into the range from 0 to 1 (a negative sum gives 0). That is nearly all of it.

The words *neuron* and *cell* mean the same thing in this book.

## Exciting and inhibiting

A synapse can push its target up or down. An **excitatory** neuron raises the activity of every neuron it
reaches; an **inhibitory** neuron lowers it. A real neuron is one or the other, never both (this is called
*Dale's law*), and the brains in this book follow that rule.

Inhibition is not just "the minus sign". It is how a brain says *not now*, and most of the circuits in this book
are built from three small patterns:

```{=html}
<figcaption class="lb-caption">Filled circles fire, pale circles are silent; red-edged circles are inhibitory. An arrowhead
excites its target, a bar inhibits it.</figcaption>

```

- **Excitation** passes a signal on: *this is food, so bite*.
- **A gate** is an inhibitory cell that holds an action back until a condition is met. In the valence stage, a
  cell that fires whenever nothing is within reach holds the bite shut, so that wanting to eat does not turn into
  biting the air.
- **Disinhibition** switches a gate off, and that releases the action. Brains use it a lot: rather than pushing an
  action into being, they keep many actions held back and lift the hold on one.

A fourth pattern appears later: **competition**, where cells inhibit each other so that only the strongest few stay
active.

## Reading a brain diagram

Every stage page shows the brain of that stage. Here is the brain of the valence stage, the second one:

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="1.1"></div>

- A **box** is a group of neurons with one job, called a **region**: the eyes, the motor neurons that move the
  creature, a cell for pain. Its name says what it is for.
- An **arrow** between two boxes is a **projection**: all the synapses from one region onto another. The end of
  the arrow says what it does: an arrowhead excites, a bar inhibits, and a dot (on arrows from the senses) means a
  mix of both.
- The **colour** of an arrow says where its strengths come from (next section), and its **width** how strong it
  is overall.
- Under a box's name: whether its cells excite or inhibit, and how many there are. The coloured backgrounds
  group regions that belong together.
- A box outlined in green is new in this stage. The diagram opens on the *new circuit*: what the stage added and
  what it connects to directly, with the groups it does not touch drawn as empty outlines. *All cells* shows the
  other cells too, faded; *everything* shows the whole brain.

Point at a box or an arrow, or tap it on a phone, for details. You do not need to follow every arrow. Each page
says in words which arrows matter, and the rest is the brain of earlier stages.

## Where strengths come from

| arrow | origin | changes | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| dark | **designed** (hard-wired): we wire it, evolution may only make it stronger or weaker as a whole | over generations, as a whole | pain → the "this is bad" cells |
| grey | **evolved**: which synapses exist and how strong each is is inherited, with mutations | over generations, synapse by synapse | eyes → motor neurons |
| purple | **learned**: it starts where evolution left it and changes during a life | within one life | the look of a berry → "this is bad", after it hurt |

Designed connections give a cell a fixed meaning that later stages can rely on: a cell that is wired to pain and
nothing else *means* pain. Evolved connections are where evolution finds its own solutions, often in ways that are
hard to read. Learned connections are the only memory a creature has of its own life.

### Learning within a life

The learning in this book follows one recipe, found in real animals from sea slugs to mammals. A synapse that was
just active leaves a short **trace**. When something important happens, such as pain, a **teaching signal** is
sent to many synapses at once, and only the ones that carry a trace change. Pain says *something bad happened*;
the trace says *and this is what was there*.

### Modulators

Some cells do not talk to one partner through a synapse. They release a **neuromodulator**, a substance that
spreads and reaches many cells at once, and that is cleared slowly. Serotonin and dopamine are the best-known.
Modulators set the mood of a brain more than its next move: because they linger, they let an event act on
behaviour for a while after it is over. In the diagrams they are drawn in pink.

## Evolution

Evolution here is a **genetic algorithm**. A **genome** is what a creature inherits: the strengths of its evolved
synapses and a few settings, such as how fast it learns. A **population** of genomes is born into a world, each as
a few identical creatures. The **fitness** of a genome is how well its creatures did: here, roughly, how long they
lived with a full stomach. The genomes that did best have children, each from two parents, with small random
changes (**mutations**). That is one **generation**, and a stage runs for about a hundred of them.

Nobody tells evolution what a circuit is for. If a new cell helps, the genomes that use it have more children; if
it does not, evolution may turn it down or ignore it.

## Reading the experiments

Each stage asks one question: **does the new circuit get used?** Three tools answer it.

- **Main against control.** *Main* is the new brain. The *control* is the brain of the previous stage, in the
  same new world, starting from the same population. Whatever separates them is the new circuit, so every
  comparison on a stage page is new brain against old brain.
- **Lesions.** At the end, a region of the evolved brain is silenced and the creatures live again. If they do much
  worse, they were using it. This is the main evidence on every page.
- **Seeds.** Evolution is noisy: one run can end almost anywhere. So every stage is run three times from different
  random starts (*seeds*). A result counts only when it holds in all three.

Results are given as a mean over the seeds with a **standard error** (±): roughly, how far the mean might move if
the experiment were run again. A difference smaller than about twice its standard error could be luck.
[How a stage is judged](index.qmd#sec-judged) on the introduction page says more.

## Glossary

| term | meaning |
|---|---|
| creature | one simulated individual; *animal* always means a real one |
| tick | one step of the simulation, about a second of behaviour |
| look | what a creature sees of a thing: a short list of numbers, like a colour |
| neuron, cell | a unit with an activity between 0 (silent) and 1 (firing fast) |
| synapse, strength | a connection between two neurons, and how much it counts |
| excitatory, inhibitory | raises or lowers the activity of the neurons it reaches |
| region | a group of neurons with one job, a box in the diagram |
| projection | all synapses from one region onto another, an arrow in the diagram |
| hard-wired | designed; evolution tunes only its overall strength |
| evolved | inherited synapse by synapse, shaped by selection |
| learned, plastic | changes within a life |
| motor neurons | the cells that move the creature: step, turn, bite |
| motor programme | a cell that triggers a whole action, such as biting |
| gate | an inhibitory cell that holds an action back until a condition is met |
| disinhibition | releasing an action by silencing its gate |
| valence | sorting things into good (*appetitive*) and bad (*aversive*) |
| unconditioned stimulus | something that matters without learning, such as pain or taste |
| adaptation | a sense reporting change rather than level: what stays the same fades |
| modulator | a substance released by a few cells that acts on many, slowly |
| genome | what a creature inherits |
| fitness | what selection rewards: here, the well-fed lifetime |
| generation | one round of living, selecting and breeding |
| seed | one independent run of a stage, from its own random start |
| main, control | the new brain, and the previous brain in the same new world |
| lesion | silencing a region to see whether the creatures need it |
| ± (standard error) | how far a mean might move if the experiment were repeated |
